mainTopic: Extra money in a payment that may be a mistake or a hidden repayment of theft, and ריבית in advance purchases of growing produce (gourds, milk, wool) and wine.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a rule about extra money found in a payment. If the extra fits counting in tens or fives, we assume it was a mistake. רב אחא בריה דרבא asks רב אשי about a harsh giver who never gives gifts, and then about a stranger who never dealt with the receiver. Both times רב אשי answers that the extra may be stolen money being quietly returned. He backs this with a ברייתא: a thief who slips the stolen amount into a calculation has fulfilled his duty. Next, רב כהנא tells how he heard רב say "קרי קרי" (gourds). The students explain that paying a gardener now for bigger gourds later is ריבית unless the big gourds already exist, even though gourds grow by themselves. A ברייתא about selling a set amount of milk, wool and honey supports this. In another version רבא permits the sale, and he answers the ברייתא: milk and wool are new produce that replaces what was taken, while a gourd itself grows. Finally אביי permits paying in advance for wine when the buyer takes the price risk, and רב שרביא begins to challenge him on the next amud.

steps.title: The kind of amount people mistake: tens and fives
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes the previous discussion. Extra money counts as a mistake when it fits counting in groups of ten or five.
steps.simpleTranslation: For example, in tens or fives.
steps.whatsHappening: This short line finishes an answer that began before this section. It tells us which amounts of extra money we assume were a counting mistake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People often count coins in stacks of ten or five. If the extra amount matches a whole stack, it is easy to believe the giver slipped and added an extra stack. So we treat that extra money as a mistake, not as a gift.

keyTerms.meaning: Groups of ten (counting coins by tens)
Groups of five (counting coins by fives)

phrases.english: In tens and fives.
phrases.notes: He means the extra matches a stack of ten or five coins, so it looks like a counting slip.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes an answer that began earlier, about which extra amounts count as a mistake.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Amounts that fit counting in tens or fives are treated as a mistake.

steps.title: What if the giver is a tough person who never gives gifts?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרבא asks רב אשי about a giver known as harsh and stingy. The extra money can't be a gift, and it doesn't fit a counting mistake either.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא the son of רבא said to רב אשי: And if he is a harsh person who doesn't give gifts, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא asks a follow-up question. What happens when the extra money doesn't look like a mistake, but the giver is someone who would never give a present?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier rule had two options. Either the extra was a counting mistake, or it was a gift. Here the gift option seems impossible because this person never gives gifts, so we need to know how to treat the money.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Acha the son of Rava said to Rav Ashi:
And if he is a harsh person,
phrases.notes: "He" is the one who handed over the money with the extra in it.

phrases.english: who doesn't give gifts, what then?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אִינִישׁ תַּקִּיפָא הוּא דְּלָא יָהֵיב מַתָּנָה, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the mistake-or-gift rule on a giver who would never give a gift.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How do we explain extra money from someone who never gives gifts, when the amount doesn't look like a counting mistake?

steps.title: Maybe he once stole and is quietly paying it back
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the tough person may have stolen from the receiver in the past. Now he is slipping the stolen amount back into the payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Perhaps he once robbed him and slipped it into the calculation.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a third explanation for the extra money. It may be a hidden return of something the giver once stole.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now there is a new option beyond a mistake or a gift. The giver might be returning stolen money without admitting the theft. So the receiver may still keep the money even though the giver is stingy.

keyTerms.meaning: He slipped it into the calculation (hid it inside the total)

phrases.english: He said to him: Perhaps he once robbed him,
phrases.notes: רב אשי is answering. "Him" is the person who got the extra money.

phrases.english: and slipped it into the calculation for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דִּלְמָא מִיגְזָל גַּזְלֵיהּ וְאַבְלַע לֵיהּ בְּחֶשְׁבּוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the harsh person.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra may be stolen money returned secretly inside the calculation.

steps.title: A ברייתא: paying back stolen money inside a calculation counts
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי supports his answer with a ברייתא. A גזלן who returns the stolen amount hidden inside a calculation has fulfilled his duty.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: One who robs his fellow and slips it into a calculation for him has fulfilled his obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי brings a source to show his answer is realistic. The ברייתא says this kind of hidden repayment really works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might ask whether a hidden return is enough, since the victim never knew he was being paid back. The ברייתא says it is enough: the גזלן is יצא. So it makes sense that a thief would pay back this way, and that explains the extra money.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught (in a ברייתא)

steps.whatToRemember: Extra money may be a mistake, a gift, or a hidden return of stolen money. A hidden return still fully counts as paying back the theft.

phrases.english: As it was taught: One who robs his fellow
and slipped it into a calculation for him has fulfilled his obligation.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: הַגּוֹזֵל אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ וְהִבְלִיעַ לוֹ בְּחֶשְׁבּוֹן – יָצָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב אשי's answer with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That returning stolen money hidden inside a calculation is a real, valid way to pay it back.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא: הגוזל את חבירו והבליע לו בחשבון יצא

steps.title: What if the giver is a total stranger?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא asks again. What if the giver came from outside and never did business with the receiver, so he could never have stolen from him?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it is a person who comes from outside, who never did business with him, what then?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא pushes further with a new case. Here the stolen-money explanation seems impossible, because the two people never had any dealings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי's answer needed some past contact, so that the giver could have stolen from the receiver. A stranger had no such contact. So it seems the extra must just be a mistake.

keyTerms.meaning: Did business with (literally, took and gave)

phrases.english: And if it is a person who comes from outside,
who doesn't do business with him, what then?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אִינִישׁ דְּאָתֵי מֵעָלְמָא, דְּלָא שָׁקֵיל וְטָרֵי בַּהֲדֵיהּ, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests רב אשי's stolen-money answer on a case where it seems impossible.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How do we explain extra money from a stranger who could never have stolen from the receiver?

steps.title: Maybe someone else stole and asked the stranger to pay it back
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that a different person may have stolen from the receiver. That thief asked the stranger to slip the money in whenever the receiver borrows from him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Perhaps another person robbed him and said to him: When so-and-so borrows money from you, slip it into the calculation for him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אشי stretches his explanation to fit the stranger. The real thief could be returning the money through the stranger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even without direct contact, a thief could send the money back through a third person. So the stranger's extra coins can still be a hidden return of stolen money. A thief might choose this way to avoid the shame of admitting what he did.
steps.whatToRemember: Even when the giver is a stranger, the extra money could be stolen money returned through him on someone else's behalf.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דִּלְמָא אִינִישׁ אַחֲרִינָא גַּזְלֵיהּ,
phrases.english: He said to him: Perhaps another person robbed him,

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ: כִּי יָזֵיף פְּלוֹנִי פְּשִׁיטֵי מִינָּךְ
phrases.english: and said to him: When so-and-so borrows coins from you,
phrases.notes: The thief is talking to the stranger. "So-and-so" is the victim.

phrases.english: slip it into the calculation for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דִּלְמָא אִינִישׁ אַחֲרִינָא גַּזְלֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the stranger question by adding a third party to the stolen-money explanation.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A different thief may have arranged for the stranger to return the stolen money inside a loan calculation.

steps.title: רב כהנא hears רב say "קרי קרי" and doesn't understand
steps.stepSummary: A new section begins. רב כהנא tells how he sat at the far end of רב's study hall and heard רב say "gourds, gourds" without knowing what it meant.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: I was sitting at the far end of רב's study hall, and I heard him saying "gourds, gourds," and I didn't know what he was saying.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a story told by רב כהנא. It is setting up a question about what רב meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב כהנא heard only two words, "קרי קרי," because he was sitting far away. Without the full discussion he couldn't tell what the words were about. The next step asks for the explanation.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said:
I was sitting at the far end of Rav's study hall,
and I heard him saying "gourds, gourds,"
and I didn't know what he was saying.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא: הֲוָה יָתֵיבְנָא בְּשִׁילְהֵי פִּרְקֵי דְּרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, separate from the extra-money discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב said "קרי קרי" and רב כהנא didn't understand what it referred to.

steps.title: רב כהנא asks the students what רב meant
steps.stepSummary: After רב got up, רב כהנא asked the other students what "קרי קרי" meant.
steps.simpleTranslation: After רב got up, I said to them: What is the "gourds, gourds" that רב was saying?
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא asks the students to explain רב's words. The next step gives their answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This question opens the new discussion. The students who heard the whole lesson will explain what case the gourds were about.

phrases.english: After Rav got up, I said to them:
What is the "gourds, gourds" that Rav was saying?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּתַר דְּקָם רַב, אָמְרִי לְהוּ: מַאי ״קָרֵי קָרֵי״ דְּקָאָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רב כהנא asks for the meaning of the words he described in the story.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What did רב mean by "קרי קרי"?

steps.title: The students explain what רב said about gourds
steps.stepSummary: The students tell רב כהנא that רב was talking about paying a gardener in advance for gourds that will grow bigger.
steps.simpleTranslation: They told me that רב was saying this: someone gives money to a gardener for gourds. Right now ten small gourds, each a span long, sell for a coin. The gardener says, 'I will give you gourds a cubit long for that price.' If such big gourds already exist, it is permitted. If they don't exist yet, it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The other students answer רב כהנא's question from Step 8 by explaining what רב's lesson about 'gourds' was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyer pays now at the small-gourd price, and the gardener promises big gourds later. If the big gourds are already there, it is a normal sale. If he only gets bigger gourds because the buyer waited after paying early, that extra counts as ריבית, payment for the waiting.

keyTerms.meaning: a span (the width of a spread hand)
they exist / they do not exist

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the rule the rest of the section discusses: paying early for goods that grow bigger later can count as ריבית.

phrases.english: They said to me: This is what Rav was saying:
Someone who gives money
to a gardener for gourds,

phrases.aramaic: וְקָא אָזְלִי עֲשָׂרָה קָרֵי בְּנֵי זַרְתָּא,
phrases.english: and they were going at ten gourds a span long (for a coin),
phrases.notes: This is today's market price for the small gourds.

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ: יָהֵבְינָא לָךְ בְּנֵי גַרְמִידָא,
phrases.english: and he said to him: I will give you ones a cubit long,
if they exist, it is permitted;
if they do not exist, it is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב כהנא's question about what 'קרי קרי' meant.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Paying in advance for bigger gourds is allowed only if the bigger gourds already exist.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Advance payment for gourds that will grow larger is forbidden unless the larger gourds already exist.

steps.title: Isn't this obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב needed to teach something so obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't this obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's ruling as too obvious to need saying. This sets up the next step, which explains the new point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Getting more goods because you paid early looks like plain ריבית. So the גמרא asks what new idea רב is adding.

phrases.english: It is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why רב's ruling in Step 9 needed to be said.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Receiving extra goods in return for paying early is clearly ריבית, so the ruling seems to add nothing new.

steps.title: Growth that happens by itself still counts
steps.stepSummary: We might have thought it is allowed because the gourds grow on their own, so רב teaches that it is still forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said that since the gourds grow bigger by themselves, it is fine. So רב teaches us that it is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the 'it's obvious' challenge by showing the new point in רב's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The gardener does no extra work. The gourds simply grow while the buyer waits. רב teaches that even growth that happens by itself counts as ריבית when the bigger product does not exist yet at the time of payment.

phrases.english: You might have said:
since they grow bigger by themselves,
it is fine;
so he teaches us (that it is not).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the new point the ruling adds (a 'מהו דתימא')
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Growth that happens by itself, with no work from the seller, should not count as ריבית.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even natural growth counts as ריבית if the bigger product does not exist when the money is paid.

steps.title: Whose view does רב follow?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which earlier opinion matches רב's ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: In line with whom (did רב rule)?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which earlier source agrees with רב. This sets up the next step, where it brings a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that רב's point is clear, the גמרא looks for an older teaching that holds the same view about things that grow by themselves.

phrases.english: In line with whom?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Looks for an earlier source that agrees with the ruling explained in Step 11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which earlier opinion רב's ruling follows.

steps.title: Selling whatever the animals produce is allowed
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that selling 'whatever' milk, wool or honey comes out, with no set amount, is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like this תנא, as a ברייתא teaches: someone went to milk his goats, shear his sheep, or take honey from his hive. His friend met him, and he told the friend: 'Whatever my goats give is sold to you, whatever my sheep give is sold to you, whatever my hive gives is sold to you.' This is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to show that רב follows this תנא. Here is the ברייתא's first case, where the sale is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seller promises no set amount. The buyer gets whatever comes out, more or less, so he is not guaranteed extra for paying early. That is why this sale is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: a sage of the משנה era
to take honey out of a hive

phrases.english: Like this tanna.
As it is taught: One who goes to milk his goats,
or to shear his sheep,
or to take the honey from his hive,
and his friend met him, and he said to him:
Whatever my goats give in milk is sold to you,
whatever my sheep give in wool is sold to you,
whatever my hive gives in honey is sold to you;
it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the answer to Step 12 by quoting the ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רב's ruling that natural growth can count as ריבית
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about selling the milk, wool and honey that will come out

steps.title: Selling a set amount is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: if the seller promises a set amount of the produce, the sale is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he said: 'Such-and-such an amount of what my goats give is sold to you, such-and-such of what my sheep give, such-and-such of what my hive gives,' it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives its second case, which is the opposite of the first. Once a fixed amount is promised for early payment, the sale is forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the buyer is promised a set amount at today's price for produce that is not here yet. He is guaranteed to come out ahead for paying early, so the sale is forbidden.
steps.confusionAlert: The only difference between the two cases is the words 'כך וכך', a set amount. 'Whatever comes out' is allowed. A promised amount is forbidden.

phrases.english: But if he said to him:

phrases.aramaic: מַה שֶּׁעִזַּי חוֹלְבוֹת כָּךְ וְכָךְ מָכוּר לָךְ,
phrases.english: Such-and-such of what my goats give is sold to you,

phrases.aramaic: מַה שֶּׁרְחֵלַי גּוֹזְזוֹת כָּךְ וְכָךְ מָכוּר לָךְ,
phrases.english: such-and-such of what my sheep give is sold to you,

phrases.aramaic: מַה שֶּׁכַּוַּורְתִּי רוֹדָה כָּךְ וְכָךְ מָכוּר לָךְ –
phrases.english: such-and-such of what my hive gives is sold to you;
it is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא with the contrasting forbidden case.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The forbidden case in the ברייתא: a set amount of produce that does not yet exist

steps.title: Things not yet in existence are forbidden, even if they grow by themselves
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out the lesson of the ברייתא: even though milk, wool and honey come by themselves, the sale is forbidden because they did not exist at the time.
steps.simpleTranslation: So even though they grow by themselves, since they do not exist at that time, it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what the ברייתא proves and ties it back to רב's ruling about the gourds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Milk, wool and honey come on their own, just like the gourds grow on their own. Still, the ברייתא forbids the sale because the produce did not exist yet when the money was paid. This is the same idea as רב's rule.
steps.whatToRemember: Paying early for a fixed amount of goods that do not exist yet is ריבית, even if the goods come about by themselves. If they already exist, it is fine.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that ריבית is not only about the seller doing extra work. What matters is whether the goods existed when the money was paid.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּמִמֵּילָא קָא רָבוּ,
phrases.english: And even though they grow by themselves,
since they do not exist at that time,
it is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּמִמֵּילָא קָא רָבוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the lesson from the ברייתא in Steps 13-14 and connects it to רב's ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב follows this תנא: goods that grow on their own still count as ריבית if they did not exist at the time of the early payment.

steps.title: Another version: רבא permits because the gourds grow by themselves
steps.stepSummary: In a second version of the discussion, רבא rules that selling the growing gourds is permitted, because they grow by themselves.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say רבא said: since they grow on their own, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of the discussion. In this version רבא says the gourd sale is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, the fact that the gourds grow by themselves was not enough to permit the sale. In this version, that same fact is exactly the reason to permit it. The growth happens on its own, so the buyer is not getting paid extra for waiting on his money.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who say (introduces a second version)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new argument added to the first version. It is a different report of the same discussion, and it reaches the opposite ruling.

phrases.english: There are those who say: Rava said:
since they grow by themselves,
it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of the discussion. Here רבא permits the gourd sale, the opposite of the conclusion in steps 11 and 15. The ברייתא of steps 13-14 still stands, and step 17 raises it against רבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Selling growing gourds is permitted, since their growth happens on its own.

steps.title: Challenge from the ברייתא about a set amount
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא from the ברייתא that forbids selling a set amount of milk or wool.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the ברייתא teaches that a set amount is forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבא's ruling using the ברייתא quoted earlier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Milk and wool also come on their own, yet the ברייתא forbids promising a set amount of them. So "it grows by itself" should not be enough to permit the gourd sale either.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: But isn't it taught:
"Such and such an amount: forbidden"!
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא from steps 13-14 about milk, wool and honey.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's ruling from step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's reasoning that natural growth makes the sale permitted
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Milk and wool also come on their own, yet a set-amount sale of them is forbidden, so natural growth alone cannot permit a sale.

steps.title: Milk is replaced, but a gourd itself grows
steps.stepSummary: Milk and wool are new items that replace what was taken. A gourd is the same item getting bigger.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, milk and wool are not growth of the original item, because when you take some, new milk or wool comes in its place. Here, the gourd itself grows, because when you pick it, no new gourd replaces it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing that the gourds and the milk and wool are different kinds of cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Milk and wool that come later are brand-new produce that did not exist at the time of the sale. A gourd's later growth is just the same gourd getting bigger. The buyer already owns that gourd, so its growth is simply his.

keyTerms.meaning: From it, from the item itself

steps.whatToRemember: In this version, a sale is permitted when the thing sold is itself what grows (gourds). A set amount is forbidden when the produce is new and replaces what was taken (milk, wool).

phrases.english: There, they do not grow from the item itself,
phrases.notes: "There" is the milk and wool of the ברייתא.

phrases.english: for they take this one
and another comes in its place.
Here, they grow from the item itself,
for when they take this one,
no other comes in its place.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 17.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Anything that comes on its own should be treated the same as milk and wool.
steps.terutzMaskana: Milk and wool are new, replacing produce. A gourd's growth is part of the same gourd the buyer already owns, so the sale is permitted.

steps.title: אביי: paying in advance for a barrel of wine
steps.stepSummary: אביי permits paying now for a future barrel of wine. The seller takes the risk of souring, and the buyer takes the risk of price changes.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: A person may say to his friend, "Here are four zuz for a barrel of wine. If it sours, that is your loss. If the price goes up or down, that is on me."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. אביי rules on a case of paying in advance for wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyer pays now and gets the wine later, which could look like a loan repaid with extra (ריבית). But here the buyer accepts the ups and downs of the price, so he is not guaranteed a profit. The seller stays responsible only if the wine itself spoils.

keyTerms.meaning: In your domain (your risk) / in my domain (my risk)

phrases.english: Abaye said:
It is permitted for a person
to say to his friend:
"Here are four zuz for a barrel of wine;
if it sours, it is in your domain;
phrases.notes: "In your domain" means the seller takes the loss if the wine turns to vinegar.

phrases.english: if it rises or drops in price, it is in my domain."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about paying in advance.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Paying in advance for wine is permitted when the seller bears the risk of souring and the buyer bears the risk of price changes.

steps.title: רב שרביא begins to respond to אביי
steps.stepSummary: רב שרביא turns to אביי to question his ruling. His actual words come next.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שרביא said to אביי:
steps.whatsHappening: This line is a setup. The גמרא is introducing רב שרביא's response to אביי, which continues right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing has been argued yet. This line only tells us that אביי's ruling is about to be questioned, so the learner should expect a challenge next.
